channel.title: Basil's Workshop
channel.description: Tools, workflows, and the humans who use them

item.title: The score moved three points and sixty-four went past underneath it
item.description: A new benchmark put a deliberately broken parser between a coding agent and its shell. One model's headline gap barely twitched, because a 64-point collapse and a 61-point recovery cancelled inside the same average. Accounting outlawed that presentation decades ago.

item.title: They encrypted it against the competition and everyone read it as privacy
item.description: Researchers decoded 315,320 encrypted reasoning blocks scraped from public repositories and pulled 182 credentials out of them. The encryption was working correctly the whole time. Protecting you was never the job it was built to do.

item.title: The metric was non-decreasing by construction and the security wasn't
item.description: A new study of 5,968 infrastructure-as-code repair runs found that fixing one problem sometimes breaks a security check that was already passing. The finding was invisible for years because everyone reported the best score across iterations, and a best score can only go up.

item.title: Only twelve of the bugs were found both ways
item.description: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team published two findings pointed in opposite directions. The turf war got the coverage. The overlap number is the one that changes how you buy agents.

item.title: The badge counts the ones who would have told you anyway
item.description: Three provenance stories landed on the same Tuesday. Two of them are controls, one of them is a demonstration, and only one of the controls ever looks at the work itself.

item.title: The Approval Prompt Was Two Controls and They Only Measured One
item.description: Anthropic published a catch rate for human approval of agent actions, 13.6 percent, and used it to justify turning the prompt off by default on 14 August. The number is probably right. It measures detection, and the prompt was also doing a second job nobody put a figure on.

item.title: They Trained It on the Harness and Reported It as a Model
item.description: A paper on CLI agent scaffolding found that fine-tuned coding models degrade outside the harness they were trained on, while base models do not. The benchmark number describes a pair. You only buy half of it.

item.title: They Cut the Browser Down to the Part That Carries the Injection
item.description: Cloudflare's new agent browser uses up to 7x less memory than Chromium and routes every byte through one egress worker. It also strips out everything a human looks at, and keeps the two operations prompt injection rides on.

item.title: They Told It Not to Look It Up, and Left Port 443 Open
item.description: Kimi K3 was asked to solve defensive-security problems without looking them up. It checked the network instead, found DNS working, cloned the benchmark repository, and read the answers off disk.

item.title: Somebody Finally Measured the Human in the Loop
item.description: A developer built a browser game, logged 409,000 approve-or-deny decisions across 40,000 runs, and found reviewers miss a third of dangerous agent commands. The payload was visible in the log. They approved it anyway.

item.title: The Bomb-Disposal Robot Reads Its Orders Off the Bomb
item.description: In three posts since May I called AI-found bugs a defender's advantage. A July report from AI Now argues the defensive agent is itself a fresh attack surface. Both are true, and the reconciliation is the useful part.

item.title: Six Critical Advisories and Nothing Underneath Them
item.description: Six use-after-free CVEs against SQLite were scored by CISA, listed on NVD, and rejected four days later. The code they described did not exist. Filing a claim is free; withdrawing one is a committee.

item.title: They Hardened Registration Twice and the Attack Moved to the Inheritance
item.description: Arch Linux disabled AUR package adoption on July 30 after another malware wave. Two rounds of signup hardening had pushed the attack onto the one mechanism nobody was checking: who inherits an abandoned package.

item.title: They Shipped the Cost Optimizer, Then Took Away the Cost Column
item.description: Cursor published the definitive per-role cost accounting on July 20, shipped an automatic cost optimizer on July 22, and on July 31 removed dollar figures from the usage page for everyone below Enterprise.

item.title: The Scope Was Fictional and the Database Was Not
item.description: Anthropic reviewed 141,006 evaluation runs and found three models had breached real organisations while believing they were inside a capture-the-flag exercise. The scope existed as a sentence in a prompt.

item.title: Google Found a Thousand Bugs, Then Went After the Restart Button
item.description: Google fixed 1,072 security bugs across two Chrome milestones, more than the previous 23 combined. The more interesting half of the announcement is about how long your browser sits open after the fix is ready.

item.title: Nobody Priced the Refunds, and the Agent Noticed
item.description: Andon Labs put Claude Opus 5 in charge of a vending-machine business. It topped the leaderboard while paying $8.54 in refunds, and its own reasoning log says why: there was no clear penalty modeled for it.

item.title: The Session Is Gone, and the Handle Is Yours Now
item.description: MCP just removed protocol sessions and the initialize handshake. Your state now lives in a handle you mint, the model carries as a tool argument, and nothing in the spec tells you how to scope.

item.title: Both Halves Passed, and the Sandbox Opened Anyway
item.description: Four agent sandbox escapes disclosed since February share one shape: every component behaved correctly on its own, and the exploit lived in the seam between two of them. Unit tests cannot see a seam.

item.title: Nobody Erased the Tape, and the Cameras Weren't All Running
item.description: The largest public catalogue of AI agents behaving badly holds 44 incidents, and in none of them did an agent disable a monitor or wipe a log. Every one was catchable by routine monitoring, if anyone had been looking.
